question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning given below?

To do something strictly in accordance with the official rules and procedures, allowing oneself no latitude whatever.
option_2: To be in someone’s good books
option_3: To throw the book at someone
solution_text:
The correct answer is To go by the book.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "to go by the book" means to follow the rules and procedures exactly, without exercising discretion or taking any short cut.

 

• Example: *The new inspector went by the book, and the clearance that had once taken a day now took a fortnight.*

 

• All four alternatives belong to the book family of idioms, so the answer must be decided by meaning alone.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The related expression "to work to rule" describes a form of industrial protest in which employees obey every regulation so scrupulously that work slows to a crawl — proving, in effect, that going by the book is not always the most efficient way to proceed.

 

• The opposite idea is carried by "to bend the rules" or "to cut corners".

 

NOTE

 

• To be in someone's good books (Option 2): To be in favour with someone. The image is of a ledger in which credits are recorded, and the opposite phrase is *in someone's bad books*.

 

• To throw the book at someone (Option 3): To impose the heaviest possible punishment, charging a person with every offence available. Note the trap here: this idiom also concerns strict adherence to rules, but from the side of punishment, not procedure.

 

• To be a closed book (Option 4): To be something one knows nothing about, or a person whose thoughts cannot be read. *Higher mathematics was a closed book to him.*

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning given below?

A long and foolish search for something that does not exist or cannot possibly be found.
option_2: What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander
option_3: To kill the goose that lays the golden eggs
solution_text:
The correct answer is A wild goose chase.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "a wild goose chase" means a hopeless and time-wasting pursuit of something that cannot be found, or that does not exist at all.

 

• Example: *The anonymous letter sent the inspector on a wild goose chase through three districts.*

 

• All four alternatives are genuine goose idioms, each with a settled and quite separate meaning.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The expression is found in Shakespeare's *Romeo and Juliet* (1597). It originally referred to a kind of horse race in which riders followed a leader in the scattered formation of wild geese in flight — an erratic and pointless-looking pursuit.

 

• Idioms close in sense: to chase rainbows, to look for a needle in a haystack, a fool's errand.

 

NOTE

 

• To cook someone's goose (Option 1): To ruin a person's chances or plans. *His remark to the chairman cooked his goose.*

 

• What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander (Option 2): A proverb meaning that what is fair for one party must be fair for the other — a principle of even-handedness, not a description of a futile search.

 

• To kill the goose that lays the golden eggs (Option 3): To destroy, out of greed or impatience, the source of one's own prosperity. The allusion is to Aesop's fable.

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

To carry coals to Newcastle.
option_1: To supply something to a place where it already exists in abundance
option_2: To undertake a long and exhausting journey for very little reward
option_3: To perform dirty or menial work on behalf of another person
option_4: To transport goods in a manner that is unsafe or unlawful
solution_text:
The correct answer is To supply something to a place where it already exists in abundance.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "to carry coals to Newcastle" means to take a thing to a place where there is already plenty of it — an act that is entirely pointless.

 

• Example: *Sending textbooks to a university library is carrying coals to Newcastle.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Newcastle upon Tyne was for centuries the great coal-exporting port of England, so that to bring coal *into* Newcastle was the plainest possible waste of effort. The phrase is recorded from the sixteenth century.

 

• Equivalents in other traditions carry the same idea: *to carry owls to Athens* (Greek), *to sell water by the river* (Chinese), and in India the expression "ulta chor kotwal ko daante" is sometimes offered, though it is not an exact parallel.

 

• Idioms close in sense: to gild the lily, to teach one's grandmother to suck eggs, to paint the lily.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 describes a hard journey for small reward, which is nearer to "the game is not worth the candle". The idiom in question turns on redundancy, not on hardship.

 

• Option 3 describes menial work done for another, which belongs to "to do someone's dirty work".

 

• Option 4 takes the word *carry* literally and attaches it to unlawful transport. Idioms are decided by the figurative sense, and this is the standard trap.

question: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Acquiesce.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is ACQUIESCE, meaning to accept something reluctantly but without protest.

 

• Two features must both be got right:

 

• The word begins ACQ-, with a c before the q. This is the commonest point of failure.

 

• It ends -ESCE, not *-ECE*.

 

• The full sequence is A-C-Q-U-I-E-S-C-E — note that it contains three c's worth of trouble, and that the letters *u-i-e* run in that order.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other words beginning acq-, all of which keep the c before the q: acquire, acquaint, acquit, acquisition, acquittal.

 

• The -esce ending belongs to a family of verbs meaning "to begin to be": coalesce, convalesce, effervesce, obsolesce, luminesce.

 

• The noun is acquiescence, and the adjective acquiescent.

 

NOTE

 

• Aquiesce (Option 1): Drops the c before the q, giving *aqui-* — which belongs to the water family (*aquatic*, *aquarium*), not to this word.

 

• Acquiece (Option 2): Gets the opening right but ends -ece, losing the s of *-esce*.

 

• Aquiece (Option 4): Wrong at both points — no c before the q, and the ending reduced to *-ece*.

question:
Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose the option "No replacement required".

The committee dismissed the submission as a plagerised version of an earlier study.
solution_text:
The correct answer is plagiarised.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The word in the sentence is spelt "plagerised", which is incorrect. The correct spelling is PLAGIARISED, from the verb plagiarise, meaning to take another person's work or ideas and pass them off as one's own.

 

• The stem contains the sequence -IAR-: pla-GI-AR-ise. The commonest error, seen here, is to write *-er-* for *-iar-*.

 

• The word comes from Latin plagiarius, meaning a kidnapper — one who steals another man's slave, and by extension another man's writing.

 

• Corrected sentence: *The committee dismissed the submission as a plagiarised version of an earlier study.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The noun is plagiarism, and the person who commits it a plagiarist — both keeping the -iar- of the stem.

 

• Note the distinction: plagiarism is the passing off of another's work as one's own; copyright infringement is the unauthorised use of protected material. The first is an offence against honesty, the second against law, and the two do not always coincide.

 

NOTE

 

• plagerized (Option 1): Repeats the -er- error of the given word, and merely changes the ending to the American -ized. Changing the ending does not touch the fault.

 

• plagirised (Option 2): Has the i but drops the a, giving *-gir-* for *-giar-*.

 

• No replacement required (Option 4): This would be right only if the given word were correct. Since the sentence reads "plagerised", a replacement is required.

question:
Match the word with its closest synonym.

Word: Alacrity
solution_text:
The correct answer is Eagerness.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alacrity (noun) means brisk and cheerful readiness; a prompt and willing eagerness to act.

 

• Its closest synonym among the alternatives is Eagerness.

 

• Example: *He accepted the transfer with an alacrity that surprised everybody in the office.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word carries two elements at once — speed and willingness. A man who acts quickly but grudgingly does not act with alacrity.

 

• It is almost always used in the phrase "with alacrity", and comes from Latin alacer, "lively, brisk".

 

• Other synonyms: promptness, readiness, willingness, enthusiasm, zeal.

 

NOTE

 

• Reluctance (Option 2): Means unwillingness or hesitation — the direct antonym, and the principal trap here.

 

• Confusion (Option 3): Means bewilderment or disorder. A person may act quickly and yet be confused; the two words describe different things altogether.

 

• Fatigue (Option 4): Means extreme tiredness, which is the enemy of both the speed and the willingness that alacrity implies.

question: Which of the following words is the closest synonym of the word "truculent"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Aggressive.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Truculent (adjective) means eager or quick to argue or fight; aggressively defiant.

 

• Its closest synonym among the alternatives is Aggressive.

 

• Example: *He answered every question in a truculent tone, as though each had been an accusation.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word comes from Latin trux, trucis, meaning "fierce" or "savage".

 

• Other synonyms: belligerent, pugnacious, combative, defiant, bellicose, hostile.

 

• Note the useful distinction: truculent describes a manner that is aggressive and sullen — it suggests a readiness to quarrel joined to a bad temper, which *aggressive* alone does not convey.

 

NOTE

 

• Gentle (Option 1): Means mild and kindly — the direct antonym.

 

• Cautious (Option 2): Means careful to avoid risk. It is placed here because it resembles *truculent* in no way except length — a reminder that hard words must be known, not guessed.

 

• Cheerful (Option 3): Means in good spirits. Truculence carries a note of sullenness, so this points the wrong way, though it is not the exact opposite.

question:
There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.

The superintendent confirmed that all correspondance had been acknowledged and duly forwarded.
solution_text:
The correct answer is correspondance.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The misspelt word is "correspondance". The correct spelling is CORRESPONDENCE, meaning letters and communications exchanged between persons.

 

• The ending is -ENCE, not *-ance*. The word is built on correspond, and the pattern is correspond → correspondence.

 

• Note also the double R in the middle: cor-RE-spond-ence.

 

• Corrected sentence: *The superintendent confirmed that all correspondence had been acknowledged and duly forwarded.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The -ence / -ance distinction is one of the hardest in English spelling, and there is no rule that covers every case. The two groups must be learnt:

 

• -ENCE: correspondence, existence, occurrence, persistence, independence, competence, patience, difference, preference, reference

 

• -ANCE: perseverance, maintenance, appearance, acquaintance, resistance, attendance, guidance, importance, assistance

 

• A useful pair to hold together: correspondence takes -ence, while maintenance and perseverance take -ance.

 

NOTE

 

• superintendent (Option 1): Correctly spelt, and note that it too ends in -ent, not *-ant* — a common error in official English.

 

• acknowledged (Option 2): Correctly spelt. Note the silent c after the a, and that the stem is the complete word *knowledge*.

 

• forwarded (Option 4): Correctly spelt, with -ward- in the middle, as in *toward*, *backward* and *onward*.

question: Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning to "placate".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Provoke.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Placate (verb) means to make somebody less angry or hostile; to soothe or calm a person who is annoyed.

 

• Its direct antonym is Provoke, meaning to stir up anger deliberately.

 

• Example: *Every attempt to placate the crowd only provoked it further.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word comes from Latin placare, "to soothe" — the same root that gives placid (calm) and implacable (impossible to soothe).

 

• Other antonyms: incense, enrage, antagonise, irritate, exasperate, inflame.

 

NOTE

 

• The question is built so that three of the four options are synonyms of the key word and only one is its opposite. Recognising that shape at once saves time.

 

• Appease (Option 1): Means to pacify by giving in to demands — a synonym, though it carries a suggestion of concession that *placate* need not.

 

• Pacify (Option 2): Means to quieten or bring peace to — the plainest synonym of the three.

 

• Mollify (Option 4): Means to soften the anger of — a third synonym, from Latin *mollis*, "soft".

question: Choose the word that is the antonym of "zenith".
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nadir.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Zenith (noun) means the highest point — in astronomy, the point of the sky directly overhead; figuratively, the peak of a person's power or success.

 

• Its direct antonym is Nadir, the lowest point — in astronomy the point directly beneath the observer, and figuratively the lowest moment of one's fortunes.

 

• Example: *The Mughal empire reached its zenith under Aurangzeb and its nadir within fifty years of his death.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Both words came into English from Arabic, by way of medieval astronomy: samt ("path") gave *zenith*, and nazir ("opposite") gave *nadir*. They are among the many astronomical terms English owes to Arabic, along with azimuth, almanac and algebra.

 

• The pair zenith / nadir is examined constantly, and is worth memorising as a unit.

 

NOTE

 

• Apex (Option 1): Means the topmost point of anything — a synonym of zenith, not its opposite.

 

• Summit (Option 2): Means the highest point of a mountain, and figuratively the highest level of achievement — a second synonym.

 

• Pinnacle (Option 4): Means the highest point of success or fame, and literally a small pointed turret. A third synonym on the same side.

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

A person who studies fossils and the forms of life that existed in prehistoric times.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Palaeontologist.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A palaeontologist is one who studies fossils and the plants and animals of prehistoric times.

 

• The word is formed from Greek palaios ("ancient") + onta ("beings") + logos ("study of") — literally *the study of ancient beings*.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Four neighbouring studies are constantly confused, and the distinction is the whole of this question:

 

• Palaeontologist – fossils and prehistoric life, including dinosaurs

 

• Archaeologist – human remains and artefacts: buildings, pottery, tools, coins

 

• Geologist – the rocks and structure of the earth itself

 

• Anthropologist – human societies, cultures and physical development

 

• A useful rule of thumb: if the subject is human and made, it is archaeology; if it is living and ancient, it is palaeontology; if it is rock, it is geology.

 

NOTE

 

• Archaeologist (Option 2): Studies the material remains of human civilisations. A dinosaur bone is not his business; a broken pot is. This is the closest distractor, and the one most often chosen wrongly.

 

• Geologist (Option 3): Studies the earth's crust, its rocks and its history. Fossils occur in rocks, so the two fields meet — but the geologist's subject is the rock, not the creature.

 

• Anthropologist (Option 4): Studies human beings and their societies, and works chiefly with the living or the recent.

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

A person who falsely claims to possess special knowledge or skill.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Charlatan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A charlatan is a person who pretends to a knowledge or skill he does not possess, usually in order to deceive others for gain.

 

• The word came into English from Italian ciarlatano, from *ciarlare*, "to chatter" — the original charlatan being a patter-selling quack who sold worthless medicines in the market place.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Words for impostors and pretenders, which are examined together:

 

• Charlatan – falsely claims knowledge or skill

 

• Quack – a charlatan specifically in medicine

 

• Impostor – falsely assumes another person's identity

 

• Hypocrite – pretends to virtues or beliefs he does not hold

 

• Sycophant – flatters the powerful for advantage

 

• Against these stand the words for genuine attainment: connoisseur, virtuoso, savant, pundit, adept.

 

NOTE

 

• Connoisseur (Option 2): An expert judge in matters of taste, especially of art, food or wine. His knowledge is real, and he claims no more than he has.

 

• Virtuoso (Option 3): A person of outstanding technical skill, especially in music. Again the accomplishment is genuine.

 

• Savant (Option 4): A person of profound learning, particularly in science or scholarship. The three distractors are placed together because each names the very thing the charlatan pretends to be.

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

The new manager soon dispensed _____ the old registers altogether.
solution_text:
The correct answer is with.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb dispense, in the sense of doing away with something as unnecessary, is always followed by with: *to dispense with formalities, to dispense with a servant, to dispense with the registers*.

 

• Completed sentence: *The new manager soon dispensed with the old registers altogether.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dispense has a second and quite different sense — to distribute or administer — in which it takes a direct object and no preposition: *the chemist dispenses medicines*, *the court dispenses justice*. A dispensary takes its name from this sense.

 

• Verbs that take with: *comply with, cope with, part with, tamper with, quarrel with, correspond with, sympathise with, dispense with*.

 

NOTE

 

• from (Option 2): Used with verbs of prevention and separation — *prevent from, refrain from, desist from, differ from*.

 

• of (Option 3): Used with verbs of removal and deprivation — *deprive of, rob of, cure of, relieve of*. The similarity of sense makes this the strongest distractor, but *dispense* does not belong to that family.

 

• off (Option 4): Off is not used with *dispense* at all. Note the unrelated *dispense* in a chemist's shop, which takes no preposition.

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

He acquiesced _____ the decision of the committee without a word of protest.
solution_text:
The correct answer is in.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb acquiesce is followed by the preposition in: *to acquiesce in a decision, in an arrangement, in a proposal*.

 

• Completed sentence: *He acquiesced in the decision of the committee without a word of protest.*

 

• Acquiesce means to accept something reluctantly but without objecting to it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Verbs taking in: *acquiesce in, persist in, succeed in, result in, believe in, specialise in, indulge in, participate in, culminate in*.

 

• Note the fine distinction in sense: to agree to a decision is to approve it; to acquiesce in a decision is to submit to it without approving. The preposition and the meaning go together.

 

NOTE

 

• to (Option 1): The strongest distractor by far, because agree to, consent to and assent to are all correct and mean much the same thing. *Acquiesce*, however, keeps its own preposition.

 

• on (Option 2): Used with *insist on*, *decide on*, *depend on*, *rely on* — a different family altogether.

 

• with (Option 3): Used with *comply with*, *concur with* and *agree with* (a person). One agrees with a person but to a proposal — and acquiesces in it.

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

The tribunal debarred him _____ practising for a period of two years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is from.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb debar is followed by the preposition from: *to debar somebody from an office, from an examination, from practising*.

 

• Completed sentence: *The tribunal debarred him from practising for a period of two years.*

 

• Debar means to exclude or prohibit somebody officially from doing something.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The prevention family, all taking from: *debar from, prevent from, prohibit from, restrain from, hinder from, discourage from, dissuade from, refrain from, abstain from*.

 

• Distinguish this family carefully from the removal family, which takes of: *deprive of, rob of, cure of, relieve of, divest of*. Both families concern loss, and the preposition is the only thing that separates them.

 

NOTE

 

• of (Option 1): The principal trap, because *deprive of* is so close in sense — a man debarred from practising is in effect deprived of his livelihood. But *debar* belongs to the prevention family, not the removal family.

 

• for (Option 2): Used with *account for, apologise for, compensate for, long for* — a different set again.

 

• against (Option 3): Used with verbs of opposition and protection — *guard against, warn against, protest against, discriminate against*.

question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the alternative that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case the first three alternatives are not found suitable, choose the last one, "No improvement required".

The findings of the survey were at variance to the conclusions drawn in the earlier report.
solution_text:
The correct answer is at variance with the conclusions.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is one of preposition. The fixed phrase is "at variance WITH", meaning differing from; in conflict with.

 

• Corrected sentence: *The findings of the survey were at variance with the conclusions drawn in the earlier report.*

 

• Phrases of this kind must be learnt whole. The preposition cannot be worked out from the meanings of the individual words, which is why examiners return to them so often.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• A group of fixed phrases built on at, all worth memorising:

 

• at variance with – in conflict with

 

• at odds with – in disagreement with

 

• at loggerheads with – in open dispute with

 

• at the mercy of – wholly in the power of

 

• at a loss for – unable to find (*at a loss for words*)

 

• at par with – equal to; at the cost of; at the expense of

 

NOTE

 

• at variance from (Option 1): The strongest distractor, since *differ from* and *different from* are both correct. But *variance* takes with, not *from*.

 

• at variance against (Option 2): Against is used with phrases of opposition and protection, never with *variance*.

 

• Option 4 cannot be right, since *"at variance to"* is not an English phrase at all.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. The village had been promised a bus service for as long as anybody could remember.
A. It ran for eleven days, and on the twelfth it did not come.
B. In the winter of that year a bus actually arrived, painted blue, with the route number chalked on a board at the front.
C. The driver, when he was found, said that the road had been declared unfit — which everybody in the village had known for thirty years.
D. Nobody at the depot could say who had sent it, and nobody was willing to say who might take it away again.
S2. The board with the route number was taken down and used to cover a broken window in the panchayat office.
solution_text:
The correct answer is BDAC.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• B must open the sequence. S1 tells us only of a promise; B supplies the event — a bus actually arrived. Every other sentence presupposes that the bus is already there.

 

• D follows B. The pronoun "it" in *"who had sent it"* refers to the bus of B, and the sentence records the puzzlement of the depot immediately after its arrival.

 

• A follows D. *"It ran for eleven days"* describes the service that then began, and ends it — *"on the twelfth it did not come"*.

 

• C must be last of the four. The driver is sought after the bus has stopped coming, and his explanation accounts for the failure described in A. The phrase *"when he was found"* also implies a search, which can only follow the disappearance.

 

• S2 closes the paragraph with the board of B being put to another use — the detail returns to where the story began, and completes the irony.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The paragraph has the shape promise → arrival → mystery → failure → explanation, and the explanation is deliberately the flattest thing in it. Where a paragraph ends on an anticlimax, the sentence carrying that anticlimax is almost always the last of the jumbled four.

 

NOTE

 

• ADBC (Option 2): Opens with A, so the bus runs for eleven days before it has arrived.

 

• CDBA (Option 3): Opens with C, so the driver explains the failure of a service that has not yet begun.

 

• BACD (Option 4): Correct at the opening, but places A before D, so the depot's puzzlement about who sent the bus comes only after the service has already ended. The natural place for that puzzlement is at the arrival, not after the disappearance.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. Miss Fernandes taught mathematics at the convent school for thirty-one years.
A. She kept it in the second drawer of her desk, and at the end of every year she added the new names to it.
B. In her last week at the school she took it out, looked at it for a long time, and put it back where it had always been.
C. What her pupils never knew was that she kept a list of every girl who had failed her examination.
D. Against each name she had written, in a very small hand, what had become of the girl afterwards.
S2. The drawer was cleared by the office three months later, and nobody who saw the list understood what it was.
solution_text:
The correct answer is CADB.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• C must open the sequence. S1 gives only the length of her service; C introduces the list, which every other sentence refers to as *"it"*. A pronoun cannot precede the noun it stands for.

 

• A follows C, telling us where the list was kept and how it grew — the drawer, and the names added each year.

 

• D follows A. Having established that the list contained names, the paragraph now records what was written against each name. D cannot precede A, because A is what introduces the accumulation of names.

 

• B must be last of the four. It carries the time marker "In her last week at the school", which is the latest point in the narrative, and its phrase *"put it back where it had always been"* refers to the drawer of A.

 

• S2 follows directly: the drawer is cleared three months afterwards.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Notice how the paragraph withholds its point. Nothing is said about why she kept the list, and S2 makes the withholding permanent — *"nobody who saw the list understood what it was"*. The reader is left to supply the explanation, which is the whole effect of the piece.

 

NOTE

 

• DBAC (Option 1): Opens with D, so we read what was written against each name before we know there is a list at all.

 

• CDAB (Option 2): Correct at both ends, but reverses A and D, so the entries against the names are described before the list is shown to have accumulated any. This is the closest of the wrong answers.

 

• ACDB (Option 3): Opens with A, whose *"She kept it"* has no antecedent — the list appears only in C, placed second here.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. The first rain of the season reached the town at four in the afternoon.
A. By five the drains had given up altogether, and the water stood a foot deep at the crossing.
B. Within ten minutes the street was empty of everything but a boy with a bicycle, pushing it slowly through the flood.
C. Shopkeepers came out to watch it, as they did every year, and stood under their awnings with their arms folded.
D. Then it began in earnest, and they went back inside and pulled the shutters halfway down.
S2. It rained for four days after that, and by the end of the week nobody in the town could remember what the dust had looked like.
solution_text:
The correct answer is CDAB.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The paragraph is governed by a clock: four o'clock (S1), the first minutes (C and D), five o'clock (A), and the ten minutes after that (B).

 

• C follows S1 directly. The pronoun "it" in *"came out to watch it"* refers to the rain of S1, and the shopkeepers' watching belongs to the first light shower.

 

• D follows C. The word "Then" marks the change — the rain begins in earnest — and "they went back inside" refers to the shopkeepers of C.

 

• A follows D. By five o'clock the drains have failed. This is later than the moments described in C and D, and is caused by the heavy rain of D.

 

• B must be last of the four. *"Within ten minutes"* counts from the flooding of A, and the empty street with the single boy is the picture the paragraph has been building towards.

 

• S2 then widens out to the four days that followed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Two devices settle this question, and both recur constantly:

 

• A pronoun must follow its noun — *"watch it"* needs the rain of S1.

 

• "Then" and "Within ten minutes" are both backward-looking markers: each needs an event already described for it to follow.

 

NOTE

 

• DBAC (Option 1): Opens with D, whose *"Then"* has nothing to follow, and whose *"they"* refers to shopkeepers not yet mentioned.

 

• CABD (Option 2): Places A before D, so the drains fail at five o'clock while the rain is still the light shower the shopkeepers were watching — the cause comes after its effect.

 

• BCDA (Option 3): Opens with B, so the street is empty ten minutes after nothing, and the shopkeepers come out to watch after the flood has already driven everyone indoors.

question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the alternative that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel the first three alternatives do not improve the sentence, then choose the last one, "No improvement required".

After the audit report was made public, the chairman found himself in hot waters.
solution_text:
The correct answer is in hot water.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is one of number within a fixed idiom. The correct form is "in hot water", with water in the singular and no article.

 

• "To be in hot water" means to be in trouble or disgrace, usually with someone in authority.

 

• Corrected sentence: *After the audit report was made public, the chairman found himself in hot water.*

 

• Idioms are fixed expressions: their words cannot be pluralised, made singular, or given articles at will, even where ordinary grammar would allow it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other idioms whose exact form must be preserved, with the commonest errors shown in brackets:

 

• *in hot water* (not *in hot waters*)

 

• *to take pains* (not *to take pain*)

 

• *by leaps and bounds* (not *by leaps and bound*)

 

• *at one's wits' end* (not *at one's wit end*)

 

• *to keep body and soul together*; *to be at daggers drawn*

 

NOTE

 

• in a hot water (Option 1): Adds the article a, which the idiom does not take, and keeps the sense of a physical quantity of water rather than of trouble.

 

• into hot waters (Option 2): Wrong twice over — into in place of *in*, and the plural retained. Note that *to get into hot water* is correct with the verb *get*, but the verb here is *found himself*, which requires *in*.

 

• Option 4 cannot be right, since the plural *waters* is not the form of the idiom.

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions based on the passage:

 

The water crisis of Indian cities is commonly described as a shortage, and it is not one. Most of the cities now rationing supply receive rainfall that would be ample if any of it were kept. The difficulty is that a city built over the last forty years is a surface from which water runs off rather than one into which it soaks: roads, roofs, parking areas and paved compounds cover ground that once absorbed the monsoon and returned it slowly to the wells. Piped supply, meanwhile, has not kept pace with the spread of the built area, and the households at the edge of a city are the last to be connected and the first to be cut off. What follows is predictable. Where the pipe does not reach, the borewell does, and every household that sinks one sinks it a little deeper than its neighbour’s. The water table falls, the shallow wells of the poorer households fail first, and those who can afford to drill again do so. A shortage that began as a failure of distribution is thus converted into a genuine scarcity, and the conversion is irreversible within any period that matters, since an aquifer emptied over thirty years is not refilled in five. The remedies proposed are three, and they are not alternatives to one another: to restore the capacity of the ground to absorb, by rainwater harvesting and by protecting the tanks and lakes that cities have built over; to extend and repair the piped network, since as much as forty per cent of treated water is lost before it reaches a tap; and to price water so that it is not wasted, while ensuring that a basic quantity reaches every household whatever it can pay. The last of these is the hardest, and no Indian city has yet managed it well.

 

According to the passage, what is the real nature of the water crisis in Indian cities?
option_1: A steady decline in the rainfall these cities receive
option_2: A sudden increase in the quantity of water each household consumes
option_3: Not a shortage of rain, but a failure to absorb it and to distribute it
option_4: A shortage of the equipment needed to drill deeper borewells
solution_text:
The correct answer is Not a shortage of rain, but a failure to absorb it and to distribute it.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage denies the usual account in its very first sentence: *"The water crisis of Indian cities is commonly described as a shortage, and it is not one."*

 

• It then gives the two real causes:

 

• Failure to absorb — a modern city is *"a surface from which water runs off rather than one into which it soaks"*, because roads, roofs and paved compounds cover ground that once took in the monsoon.

 

• Failure to distribute — *"piped supply has not kept pace with the spread of the built area"*.

 

• The passage adds that the rainfall itself *"would be ample if any of it were kept"*.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Note the force of the opening. A passage that begins by rejecting the common description of a problem is announcing that its whole argument turns on that rejection — and the examiner will almost always ask about it.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 blames the rainfall. The passage says the opposite: the rain that falls would be enough.

 

• Option 2 blames consumption. The passage nowhere mentions a rise in what each household uses.

 

• Option 4 treats drilling equipment as scarce. Borewells appear in the passage as the consequence of the crisis, and as something people are able to sink freely — not as a thing in short supply.

option_1: Households compete in sinking ever deeper borewells, and the shallow wells of the poor fail first

• The passage sets out the sequence exactly: *"Where the pipe does not reach, the borewell does, and every household that sinks one sinks it a little deeper than its neighbour's."*

 

• The consequence is then given: *"The water table falls, the shallow wells of the poorer households fail first, and those who can afford to drill again do so."*

 

• Two things are being claimed at once, and both belong in a correct answer: the competitive deepening, and the fact that the burden falls first on the poor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• What the passage describes is a familiar pattern in the use of a shared resource: each household acts sensibly for itself, and the result of all the households acting sensibly is that the resource is destroyed for everybody. The remedy cannot come from the households themselves, which is why the passage turns to public measures.

option_3: Because the piped network cannot be repaired once it has begun to leak
option_4: Because the population of a city never decreases once it has grown

• The passage gives the reason in the same sentence in which it makes the claim: the conversion *"is irreversible within any period that matters, since an aquifer emptied over thirty years is not refilled in five."*

• Note the careful qualification "within any period that matters". The passage does not say the aquifer can never recover; it says it cannot recover soon enough to be of use.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Which of the following correctly describes the remedies the passage proposes?
option_1: A single remedy: replacing all borewells with piped connections

solution_text:
The correct answer is Three remedies together: restoring absorption, repairing the network, and pricing water while guaranteeing a basic quantity.

• The passage names three, and insists that they must be taken together: *"The remedies proposed are three, and they are not alternatives to one another."*

 

• Restoring absorption — by rainwater harvesting, and by protecting the tanks and lakes that cities have built over.

 

• Extending and repairing the network — since *"as much as forty per cent of treated water is lost before it reaches a tap"*.

 

• Pricing water — so that it is not wasted, *"while ensuring that a basic quantity reaches every household whatever it can pay"*.

 

• The phrase "they are not alternatives to one another" is the key. A correct answer must convey that all three are required together.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The third remedy contains a tension the passage does not conceal: the price must be high enough to discourage waste and low enough — for a basic quantity — to reach the poorest household. Most tariff structures attempt this through a rising block rate, in which the first slab is cheap and later slabs dear.

question: भारत के योजना आयोग की स्थापना किस वर्ष तथा किस माध्यम से हुई थी?
option_1: 1950 में, भारत सरकार के एक कार्यपालिका संकल्प द्वारा
option_2: 1947 में, संविधान सभा के एक संकल्प द्वारा
option_3: 1951 में, संसद के एक अधिनियम द्वारा
solution_text:
सही उत्तर 1950 में, भारत सरकार के एक कार्यपालिका संकल्प द्वारा है।

 

महत्वपूर्ण बिंदु

 

• योजना आयोग की स्थापना 15 मार्च 1950 को भारत सरकार के एक साधारण कार्यपालिका संकल्प द्वारा हुई थी। (योजना आयोग — 15 मार्च 1950, कार्यपालिका संकल्प द्वारा)

 

• यही बिंदु इस प्रश्न का आधार है। यह आयोग:

 

• संवैधानिक निकाय नहीं था — संविधान में इसका कोई उल्लेख नहीं मिलता

 

• वैधानिक निकाय नहीं था — इसका सृजन संसद के किसी अधिनियम से नहीं हुआ था

 

• अतः यह संविधानेतर एवं गैर-वैधानिक परामर्शदात्री निकाय था, इसीलिए इसे उतनी ही सरलता से समाप्त किया जा सका जितनी सरलता से इसका सृजन हुआ था।

 

• प्रधानमंत्री इसके पदेन अध्यक्ष होते थे, तथा इसमें कैबिनेट स्तर के एक उपाध्यक्ष होते थे जो व्यवहार में इसे चलाते थे। पहले उपाध्यक्ष गुलजारीलाल नंदा थे।

 

• 1 जनवरी 2015 को इसका स्थान नीति आयोग ने ले लिया — वह भी एक कार्यपालिका संकल्प द्वारा।

 

अतः सही उत्तर विकल्प 1 है।

 

अतिरिक्त जानकारी

 

• 1952 में स्थापित राष्ट्रीय विकास परिषद (NDC) का सृजन भी इसी प्रकार कार्यपालिका संकल्प द्वारा हुआ था। इसमें प्रधानमंत्री, केंद्रीय मंत्री, सभी राज्यों के मुख्यमंत्री तथा योजना आयोग के सदस्य सम्मिलित थे, और यही प्रत्येक पंचवर्षीय योजना को अंतिम स्वीकृति देती थी।

 

• इसके विपरीत वित्त आयोग एक संवैधानिक निकाय है, जो अनुच्छेद 280 के अंतर्गत स्थापित होता है और जिसकी नियुक्ति राष्ट्रपति प्रत्येक पाँच वर्ष में करते हैं।

 

नोट

 

• विकल्प 2 (1947, संविधान सभा): संविधान सभा ने संविधान बनाया; उसने योजना आयोग का सृजन नहीं किया। के.सी. नियोगी के नेतृत्व में 1946 में एक परामर्शदात्री योजना मंडल अवश्य बना था, किंतु वह भिन्न निकाय है।

 

• विकल्प 3 (1951, संसद का अधिनियम): 1951 वह वर्ष था जब प्रथम पंचवर्षीय योजना प्रस्तुत हुई — किंतु आयोग स्वयं वैधानिक नहीं था, और इसके विषय में यही सबसे सामान्य भ्रांति है।
